From awk (“odd, clumsy”) + -ward. Compare Middle English aukeward (“in the wrong direction”).

s.d: Someone or something that is awkward.
x: Another important branch of deportment was to seat the awkwards stiffly on the extreme edge of a chair, fold the hands on the very precarious lap, droop the eyes in a pensive way.
That is a way to make awkwards. And it's not fun to hang out with awkwards more than once.

s.d: causing inconvenience
x: they arrived at an awkward time

s.d: lacking grace or skill in manner or movement or performance
x: an awkward dancer
an awkward gesture

s.d: difficult to handle or manage especially because of shape
x: an awkward bundle to carry
a load of bunglesome paraphernalia

s.d: not elegant or graceful in expression
x: an awkward prose style
a clumsy apology

s.d: hard to deal with; especially causing pain or embarrassment
x: awkward (or embarrassing or difficult) moments in the discussion
an awkward pause followed his remark

s.d: socially uncomfortable; unsure and constrained in manner
x: awkward and reserved at parties
ill at ease among eddies of people he didn't know

s.d: Lacking dexterity in the use of the hands or of tools.
x: John was awkward at performing the trick. He'll have to practice to improve.

s.d: Not easily managed; embarrassing.
x: That was an extremely awkward moment. Everyone was watching.
An awkward silence had fallen.

s.d: Lacking social skills, or uncomfortable with social interaction.
x: I'm very awkward at parties.

s.d: Perverse; adverse; difficult to handle.
x: He's a right awkward chap.
These cabinets are going to be very awkward when we move.

awl.e: From Middle English aul, alle, al, from Old English æl, from Proto-West Germanic *al, from Proto-Germanic *alaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ólos. Cognate with Saterland Frisian Äil (“awl”), Dutch aal (“awl”), German Low German Ahl (“awl”), German Ahle (“awl”), Icelandic alur (“awl”). Spelling was influenced by the Old English synonym awel, awul (“awl”), from Proto-West Germanic *ahwal, from Proto-Germanic *ahwalaz (“fork, hook”), of unknown origin. Doublet of elsen.

s.d: a pointed tool for marking surfaces or for punching small holes

A pointed instrument for piercing small holes, as in leather or wood; used by shoemakers, saddlers, cabinetmakers, etc. The blade is differently shaped and pointed for different uses, as in the brad awl, saddler's awl, shoemaker's awl, etc.
x: He dressed himself in some old ragged clothes, and took a tame white bear, which he had, with him, as well as an awl, some pitch, and twine.

s.d: Any of various hesperiid butterflies.
shaped like an awl
devoid of any feeling of awe or reverence
neither feeling nor showing respect
small aquatic plant having tufted awl-shaped leaves in a basal rosette and minute white flowers; circumboreal
(uncountable) An aquatic plant, Subularia aquatica, with awl-shaped leaves.

awn.e: Inherited from Middle English aw(u)ne, agune, from Old Norse ǫgn (compare Danish avne), from Proto-Germanic *aganō, *ahanō (“chaff”) (compare Old English agnu, Dutch agen, German Ahne, Agen), from Proto-Indo-European *aḱanā (compare Latin agna (“ear of wheat”), Lithuanian ašni̇̀s (“edge, blade”), Czech osina, Ancient Greek ἄκαινα (ákaina, “spike, prick”), ἄκανος (ákanos, “pine-thistle”), Sanskrit अशनि (aśáni, “thunderbolt, arrow tip”)), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ- (“sharp”). More at edge.

s.d: slender bristlelike appendage found on the bracts of grasses
The bristle or beard of barley, oats, grasses, etc., or any similar bristlelike appendage; arista.
x: In one exotic genus, Aristida, the awn is compound, having three forks or branches; another exotic genus, Pappophorum, is remarkable in having the flowering glume armed with a dozen or more awns.

s.d: having awns i.e. bristlelike or hairlike appendages on the flowering parts of some cereals and grasses
x: awned wheatgrass

s.d: Furnished with an awn, or long bristle-shaped tip; bearded.
x: ... between three roses seeded and awned proper, a chevron gules, ...
[…] commonly two-awned ; but in some flowers the awns are nearly obsolete; in others there are[…]

awning.e: 1615-25 (nautical sense only); from *awn + -ing, reduction of Middle French auvans (“sloping roof”), from Old French anvant (1180), from Gaulish *an(de)bannā (“eaves”) (compare Occitan ambans (“parapet”)), form of *ande- (intensive prefix) (compare Welsh an-, Old Irish ind-) + *bandā (“horn; peak”) (compare Welsh ban, Irish beann).

s.d: a canopy made of canvas to shelter people or things from rain or sun
A rooflike cover, usually of canvas, extended over or before any place as a shelter from the sun, rain, or wind.
x: At Nairobi the mail waits an hour-and-a-half. The station has three long platforms, mostly covered in awnings, the island connected with the main platform (which is used by the mails in both directions) by a subway.
A few hundred yards across the pampa from where Chilean soldiers patrol the boundary, stern-faced, the Peruvian border police sit under wind-torn blue awnings, eyeing the Chileans warily.

s.d: That part of the poop deck which is continued forward beyond the bulkhead of the cabin.
a deck at the top of a passenger ship

s.d: not functioning properly

s.d: Turned or twisted toward one side; crooked, distorted, out of place; wry.
